content: The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine has been shown to be effective in reducing the risk of leprosy, with evidence indicating a pooled risk reduction of approximately 55% when administered at birth. However, the magnitude of this protective effect varies across studies, most of which were conducted in countries with a high burden of leprosy. Despite its established efficacy, the World Health Organization (WHO) had not issued formal recommendations for the use of BCG as a leprosy prevention tool prior to the development of these guidelines. BCG is widely available and is already included in the vaccination policies of most leprosy-endemic countries. Additionally, evidence suggests that other vaccination interventions, such as those using killed mycobacteria, demonstrate similar or slightly lower efficacy compared to BCG in reducing leprosy risk. Among these, the M. indicum pranii vaccine (formerly known as M. w) is the only one currently in production. Two large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on BCG revaccination compared to a single dose at birth yielded conflicting results. One trial found no significant difference in leprosy rates between the groups, while the other reported a 49% reduction in leprosy risk with BCG revaccination compared to placebo. Consequently, the effectiveness of BCG revaccination remains unclear. Data from the COLEP SDR trial also suggest that BCG at birth may enhance the protective effect of single-dose rifampicin (SDR) chemoprophylaxis in contacts of leprosy patients. An ongoing RCT is investigating the impact of BCG revaccination in a large cohort of contacts of leprosy patients. Current conclusions shared with the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) include the following: 1. BCG administered at birth is effective in reducing leprosy risk and should continue to be used, particularly in high-burden settings (supported by good-quality evidence). 2. BCG at birth appears to enhance the protective effect of SDR in contacts, increasing protection from 57% to 80% (based on low-quality evidence). 3. The effectiveness of BCG revaccination (a second dose following the birth dose) is uncertain due to conflicting trial results. 4. Moderate-quality evidence supports the efficacy of the M. indicum pranii vaccine in preventing leprosy. The revised WHO policy on BCG for the prevention of both tuberculosis (TB) and leprosy was released in February 2018, summarizing these findings. For implementation and evaluation, the WHO Global Leprosy Programme (GLP) will collaborate with regional and country offices, as well as implementing partners, to ensure widespread dissemination of the guidelines. This will include regional and subregional events, workshops, and direct support to country program officers. The WHO will monitor the accessibility and acceptability of the guidelines during the first year of implementation, tracking downloads, hard copy requests, and distribution. The impact of the guidelines will be evaluated through epidemiological data reviews and assessments of recommendation uptake and barriers to implementation. The WHO will also monitor the effects of the recommended changes to the PB leprosy treatment regimen by evaluating treatment compliance rates. The impact of preventive SDR treatment will be assessed through disease trend analysis and incidence rates among leprosy contacts, using data collected via the annual leprosy data collection tool. These guidelines are expected to remain valid until at least 2022 unless significant new evidence necessitates an earlier review. Research priorities include the development of standardized diagnostic tools, such as PCR tests and imaging techniques, to improve leprosy diagnosis and predict disease development in contacts. Additionally, new biomarkers and more accurate diagnostic tests are needed to identify leprosy cases, particularly in subclinical stages. Further research is required to optimize treatment strategies for drug-resistant leprosy, including observational studies to evaluate alternative regimens. Trials on new and existing vaccines, such as LepVax, and combined immunoprophylaxis and chemoprophylaxis approaches are also recommended. The WHO emphasizes the need to evaluate any new TB vaccine for its potential to prevent other mycobacterial diseases, including leprosy and Buruli ulcer.
